meaning: Creator of the earth; primordial ancestor of the Yoruba

phonemes.desc: Open-mid back [ɔ] at mid tone — Yoruba's unmarked, level pitch, the calm opening of the name.
Voiced alveolar [d] plus low-tone [ù]: the pitch drops on the marked syllable and stays down.
A second, mid-tone syllable — the repetition gives the name its drum-like fall and return.
The labio-velar approximant [w] closing on low-tone [à]; the name ends where the pitch comes to rest.

pronunciation.approximation: 'oh-doo-DOO-wah' — four even syllables; the grave-marked syllables ù and à are low in pitch, sung below the others, not stressed harder.

kin.label: Yoruba exegesis
kin.form: Traditionally parsed as òdú (the great calabash of creation) + dá (to create) + ìwà (existence, character) — 'the primordial source that created existence'; the parsing is exegetical, not certain.

kin.label: Rival-brother
kin.form: Ọbàtálá / Oríṣàńlá, Olódùmarè's senior delegate, whose failure opened the way for Odùduwà's descent

kin.label: Lineage
kin.form: Ọ̀rànmíyàn (Oranyan), the youngest son and heir — founder of Ọ̀yọ́ and, by Benin court tradition, father of the first Oba of Benin

pronunciation.note: Odùduwà is Tier 1: the restored form carries the Yoruba tone marks — low ù and à — that the ASCII oduduwa cannot write. The marks are the name: a Yoruba speaker reads pitch, not spelling.

domains.title: Progenitor
domains.subtitle: Progenitor, Ile-Ife, First King
domains.lead: Odùduwà is the founder: the heaven-sent ancestor who made the earth firm, founded Ilé-Ifẹ̀, and fathered the dynasties of the Yoruba world. Every Yoruba king claims descent from him, and the Oòni of Ifẹ̀, his living heir, is the acknowledged spiritual head of the tradition.

cards.name: Progenitor
cards.desc: The primordial ancestor of Yoruba kingship — Ifẹ̀ tradition names his sons and grandsons as the founders of the Yoruba towns and their dynasties.

cards.name: Maker of the Firm Earth
cards.desc: He took the materials of creation — a handful of earth, a five-toed cockerel, a chain — and made the dry land on which the world stands (Ifá corpus; oral tradition).

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Odùduwà recovers the low tones that plain ASCII oduduwa flattens — in Yoruba, pitch is meaning.

cards.name: Ifá and Oral Attestation
cards.desc: Attested in the Ifá corpus and Yoruba oral tradition; Yoruba's Latin orthography is a nineteenth-century standardization, so the true attestation is tonal and performative, not alphabetic.

symbols.name: The chain of descent
symbols.meaning: The chain by which Odùduwà climbed down from Ọ̀run, the sky, to the primordial waters — the umbilical cord between heaven and the first city

symbols.name: The five-toed cockerel
symbols.meaning: The sacred fowl whose scratching spread the scattered handful of earth into the world's dry land

symbols.name: The handful of earth
symbols.meaning: The seed-soil of creation given by Olódùmarè — from a fistful of dust, a continent

symbols.name: Red earth of Ifẹ̀
symbols.meaning: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, 'the house of expansion' — the red soil where creation began and where his shrine still stands

symbols.name: The Ade Aare crown
symbols.meaning: The ancient crown of Ifẹ̀, worn by the Oòni only at the Olojo festival and believed by tradition to have been Odùduwà's own

mythology.lead: Odùduwà's story is the Yoruba Genesis: the descent from heaven, the making of dry land, the founding of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, and the fathering of dynasties. It lives in the Ifá corpus and in oral tradition rather than any fixed book, and the tellings disagree with one another — the tradition itself treats the variants as paths to the same city.

myths.title: Seventeen from Ọ̀run
myths.text:
In the beginning the world was water: Olódùmarè, the supreme God, ruled from Ọ̀run, the sky, while Ayé, the earth below, was soft marsh without a place to stand. The orishas petitioned to build a dry world, and Olódùmarè chose Ọbàtálá — Oríṣàńlá, the most senior among them — to lead the mission down, with Odùduwà in the company: in some tellings his younger brother, in others simply the keeper of the god's bag of materials. The delegation received what creation required — a handful of earth, a five-toed cockerel, and a chain long enough to climb from heaven to the waves. The number of the delegates shifts between tellings, sixteen or seventeen, as oral tradition allows. The story is recorded in the tellings collected by Bascom, Johnson, and Idowu from the Ifá corpus and Ifẹ̀ priests.

The myth's quiet claim is that creation in Yoruba thought is delegated: God entrusts the founding of the world to a team, and seniority alone does not finish the job. The one who climbs down will matter more than the one who was chosen to lead — and the tradition already knows it.

myths.title: The Sleep of Ọbàtálá
myths.text:
Before the descent, Ọbàtálá grew thirsty and drank palm wine — and the wine dulled him. He staggered, fell, and slept beside the work he had been sent to do. Odùduwà took the bag from his sleeping brother, climbed down the chain to the primordial waters, scattered the handful of earth onto the waves, and set the five-toed cockerel to scratching; the fowl spread the dust outward into wide dry land, beginning at the place that became Ifẹ̀. When Ọbàtálá awoke and came down to find the creation finished by another hand, the rivalry between the two worship-lines was born. Tradition adds the ritual moral: Ọbàtálá therefore forbade his priests the palm wine that undid him.

The myth explains two lasting facts at once — the founding of Ifẹ̀ and a living taboo in Ọbàtálá's cult — and its judgement is characteristic of Yoruba narrative: creation passes not to the most senior but to the most steadfast, and the instrument of failure is never an enemy, only a pleasure taken at the wrong hour.

myths.title: Where the World Began
myths.text:
The spot where Odùduwà landed and made his camp became Ilé-Ifẹ̀ — the name is usually explained as 'the house of expansion' (ifẹ̀, breadth). Here he planted his staff and raised the first city; from here the world was peopled and the kingship of the earth was administered. Ifẹ̀ tradition points to the ground of the descent to this day, and some tellings carry the quarrel upward: Ọbàtálá lodged his claim to the work with Olódùmarè, and the settlement divided the realms between them — the earth and its rule to Odùduwà, the fashioning of human bodies to Ọbàtálá. The version is old and not the only one; the tradition keeps several and argues from all of them.

Ifẹ̀'s claim to be the place where the world began is not geography but memory: the city is a monument to the act of landing. In Yoruba religious geography every road of consequence runs back to this one settlement, and the mythology exists to say why the road is there.

myths.title: The Kings Go Out
myths.text:
From Ifẹ̀, kingship radiated outward. Ifẹ̀ tradition names seven sons of Odùduwà who went out from the city to become kings of the Yoruba towns, the royal lines of the entire people descending from this single household; the youngest, Ọ̀rànmíyàn, was the heir who stayed at home longest and set out last of all. He went north and founded Ọ̀yọ́, whose Aláàfin — 'owner of the palace' — ruled the greatest of the Yoruba kingdoms. And Benin's own court tradition tells that when Benin needed a king, an embassy walked the forest road to Ifẹ̀ and was given Ọ̀rànmíyàn, whose son became the first Ọba of Benin — making Odùduwà, through his son, an ancestor of the Benin dynasty too.

The two traditions differ in detail, and modern historians debate how much of the migration narrative is memory and how much charter-myth; what no account disputes is the direction of the claim. Every dynasty wants its road to lead back to Ifẹ̀. The myth is a map of Yoruba political order, with all paths drawn to one father.

myths.title: The Crown That Came Down
myths.text:
At Ifẹ̀, Odùduwà is not only remembered; he is worshipped. His shrine stands in the sacred city, and at the Olojo festival — the feast of 'the owner of the day' — the Oòni, held to be his direct descendant, withdraws and then emerges wearing the Ade Aare, the ancient crown that tradition holds to have come down from heaven with Odùduwà himself. On this one occasion in the year the king is seen crowned, and Ifẹ̀ fills with pilgrims, chiefs, and the priests of a hundred lineages. The rite ties the city's foundation story to its living calendar: creation is not past tense at Ifẹ̀ but an annual appointment.

Each Olojo is the descent from Ọ̀run restaged in cloth, bead, and procession — the myth worn rather than told. That is the deepest sense in which Odùduwà is progenitor: the crown, the city, and the festival are one continuous inheritance, and the living king is its current syllable.

lore.syncretism: In the African diaspora the founder travelled with his people. In Brazilian Candomblé, Oxalá — the counterpart of Ọbàtálá — appears in two aspects, the young warrior Oxaguiã and the ancient creator Oxalufã, and several houses read the younger aspect as the lineal continuation of Odùduwà himself; in Cuban Santería he is remembered under the name Odudua, though Ọbàtálá dominates the liturgy. Within Nigeria the identification flows the other way: Odùduwà has been increasingly worshipped as an orisha in his own right, and in places identified with the sea-god Olókun, an association the lineages themselves debate. In the modern world the name has outgrown religion: Odùduwà functions as a pan-Yoruba symbol of common origin — on university gates, in cultural congresses, and in the political language of Yoruba identity — so that the founder has become, in effect, the patron of the idea of being Yoruba at all.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ilé-Ifẹ̀ remains the spiritual capital of the Yoruba world: the Oòni is its ritual head, chiefs from every Yoruba town pay ceremonial allegiance, and the Olojo festival draws the diaspora home. The city is also one of Africa's great art-historical sites: the naturalistic terracotta and bronze heads excavated at Ifẹ̀, dating roughly to the twelfth through fifteenth centuries, made the city famous as a medieval centre of masterly casting and modelling, and sit today in Lagos, London, and Paris. The Ifẹ̀ corpus shaped how the world studies Yoruba religion — Bascom's and Idowu's works, and the Ifá traditions themselves, made Ilé-Ifẹ̀ the reference point of the field. And in everyday life the name still does its founding work: to be Yoruba is to know the road back to Ifẹ̀, and Odùduwà is the reason the road exists. Restoring the tones of Odùduwà returns the name to the pitch in which that claim is spoken.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Odùduwà is what it means to be from somewhere. Most peoples have a founder, but few have made the founder do such concentrated work: in one figure, Yoruba tradition fuses the creation of the earth, the founding of the first city, the origin of kingship, and the common ancestry of a nation of millions. To belong, in this scheme, is not to hold a passport but to trace a road — and every king's legitimacy is measured by how convincingly his lineage walks back to Ifẹ̀.

That is why the myth resists tidy scholarly packaging: it is simultaneously cosmogony, charter, genealogy, and liturgy, and it is told in the variant voices of priests, towns, and dynasties because no single telling could hold all its jobs. The modern reader meets here the oldest political technology on record — the conversion of land into kinship. A fistful of earth, a fowl, a chain: from such small equipment, an entire people's account of itself. Every culture has such a story; Odùduwà's is among the most generous, for it makes the whole people, not a chosen line, the founder's descendants.

lore.archaeology: The material record of the myth is the city itself. Excavations at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ — beginning with Frobenius's notorious 1910 visit and continuing through the work of Willett, Eyo, and Fabunmi — uncovered the celebrated Ifẹ̀ heads: naturalistic terracotta portrait heads and copper-alloy castings of the twelfth to fifteenth centuries CE, among them the bronze heads found in 1938 in the Wunmonije compound, interpreted in tradition as the shrine images of past Oònis. The iron-crusted Opa Ọ̀rànmíyàn, a monolith over five metres tall, still stands at Ifẹ̀ as the monumental staff of Odùduwà's youngest son, and the sacred sites of the city — Odùduwà's shrine, the Olojo ground, the groves — keep the founding geography walkable. Ifẹ̀'s red earth, the stuff of the creation story, is underfoot everywhere the myth names.
